extracted.intended_audience: clergy, theological students, and educated Christians (especially Church of England ministers)
extracted.subtask_short: theological essay on religion and reason
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th‑century theological/philosophical essay concerned with the nature of true religion, the relation of reason and faith, pastoral preaching, and the correct nomenclature for speculative philosophy. It addresses how ministers and educated men should read, teach, and defend Christian doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of reason and spiritual partaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is properly the composition (interpenetration) of reason and spiritual participation — not mere speculative assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that ‘the elements (the factors) of religion are reason and understanding’ and that the sole universal preventive of all debasing superstitions is study of Old and New Testaments combined with ‘a spiritual partaking of the Redeemer's Blood’ (the sacrament). Mere rationalized understanding yields speculative faith; genuine religion requires living interpenetration of both powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as a living, generative interpenetration
rubrics_metrics.description: True/essential religion is not a balance of faculties but a living interpenetration of reason and understanding that generates a higher, vital third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with 'mechanic' philosophy (reductionist, additive). The living spiritual philosophy allows component powers to 'interpenetrate each other, and generate a higher third' giving being to essential religion; avoid treating religion as a mere theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanistic reduction of spiritual matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat spiritual life and religious truths as though they were merely the relations of unproductive particles or purely phenomenal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mechanical view 'knows only of distance and nearness, composition and decomposition' and is 'the philosophy of death.' When rules abstracted from forms in time and space are applied to spiritual being, the process becomes a gross metaphysical error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching under the influence of love
rubrics_metrics.description: A minister should speak under the influence of love and be heard under that same influence; effective preaching is affectionate and persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘How heaven-like it is to sit among brethren at the feet of a minister who speaks under the influence of love...’ Abiding spiritual knowledge infused into grateful and affectionate hearers produces growth; preaching should aim to nurture and send forth labourers into the harvest (practical evangelism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian love as evidential fruit of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian religion culminates in love, which manifests both as active good works and as patient long‑suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Christian love is the last and divinest birth... manifests itself as the sparkling and ebullient spring of well‑doing in gifts and in subservience; and as a silent fountain of patience and long‑suffering.’ This is an evaluative standard for authentic Christian life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture study combined with sacramental life
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of Scripture must be paired with sacramental/heartfelt participation to prevent superstition and secure true religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asserts that the distinction between healthy faith and superstition 'is found in the study of the Old and New Testament, if only it be combined with a spiritual partaking of the Redeemer's Blood.' This combination is presented as the practical preventive against debasing superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inward illumination over sole reliance on external knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should foster the internal 'light that lighteth every man' rather than only external learning; men should discover truths intuitively within.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When 'educated men will be ashamed to look abroad for truths that can be only found within themselves they will discover, intuitively, the distinctions between the light that lighteth every man and the understanding.' Pedagogy should cultivate receptivity to this inner light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat common sense as final arbiter in philosophical matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters that are philosophical (involving contradiction with common sense) cannot be resolved by appealing solely to common sense; they require a higher arbiter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that appeals to 'common sense as the one infallible judge' are futile in questions which are subjects of philosophy only; such disputes 'require therefore an arbiter... higher than either.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Re‑examine historical authorities with balanced sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Clergy and scholars should patiently re-hear and fairly judge predecessors' works, counterpoising prejudices with predilection for the authors, rather than dismissing them out of hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested method: 'patient re-hearing of their predecessors' cause, with enough of predilection for the men to counter‑poise the prejudices against their system'—an experimental, charitable reappraisal to recover neglected works for study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the two contagions: fanaticism and idolized unspiritual reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Be on guard against (1) fanaticism (emotional excess) and (2) idolism of an unspiritualized understanding; both are harmful but affect different temperaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text analogizes fanaticism to a fire in the flooring of the church and the idolism of the unspiritualized understanding to dry rot in the beams; remedy requires distinct responses and an integrated religious formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate criticism of contemporary infidelity with reliance on common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Attacks on modern infidels that rest on the same appeal to 'common sense' as the infidels themselves are of little lasting utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even defenders of the faith who attack infidels while appealing to common sense fail to supply the higher arbiter required; such polemics only mow down misgrowth without cleansing the soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of unreflective rejection of ancients and scholastic tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejecting all prior systems and authorities wholesale (e.g., Plato, Aristotle, Schoolmen) is dangerous; reverence for some past wisdom is warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticises the epidemic of ‘diffused sciolism’ that led to contempt for ancestors’ works and argues that the authority of the greatest names of antiquity deserves more measured treatment by clergy and scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a glossary/nomenclature for speculative philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative philosophy requires clear technical nomenclature (representation, sensation, perception, intuition, conception, fact, notion, idea) with precise senses assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author provides a glossary and states explicitly: 'I have hinted above at the necessity of a glossary, and I will conclude... with a nomenclature of the principal terms... the sense in which I have myself employed them.' Clear definitions are required for productive discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: representation / presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation (presentation) is the most general term of the speculative intellect distinguished from acts of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as umbrella term; the author introduces it as the starting point of the proposed nomenclature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: sensation (conscious presentation of subject's state)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conscious presentation that refers exclusively to the subject as a modification of his own state of being = sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensation is self‑referential presentation (subjective modification) in the glossary scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: perception (conscious presentation referring to an object)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conscious presentation that refers to an object = perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception is the presentation when it is object‑directed rather than exclusively self‑directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: intuition (immediate and individual perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: An immediate and individual perception = an intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition is direct, immediate, individualized awareness or perception in the glossary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: conception (mediate, general perception by common marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perception mediate and by means of a character or mark common to several things = a conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception is the generalizing/perceptual category formed by common marks across instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: fact / cognition (extrinsic, sensuous conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception that is extrinsic and sensuous = a fact, or a cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a conception is tied to sensuous, extrinsic referents it is labelled a fact or cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: notion (purely mental, abstracted from forms of understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception purely mental and abstracted from the forms of the understanding = a notion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A notion is an abstracted mental conception, which may become realised and thus become cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: idea (product of imagination actuated by pure reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which is neither sensation nor perception nor conception nor a notion, but an educt of the imagination actuated by the pure reason = an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An idea neither refers to outward facts nor is abstracted from the forms of perception; whether ideas are regulative only (Aristotle/Kant) or constitutive (Plato/Plotinus) is the highest problem of philosophy (beyond mere nomenclature).
